title: Development of a NETs-Related Gene Signature in Pancreatic Cancer and Validation of SLC2A1's Potential in NETs Formation.
abstract: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), DNA-protein complexes released by neutrophils, promote metastasis and immunosuppression in various cancers, but the prognostic value of NETs-related genes in pancreatic cancer (PC) remains unclear. We integrated multiple PC transcriptomic datasets from GEO with a curated NETs gene set. Differential expression analysis and WGCNA identified candidates, and three feature-selection methods (LASSO, SVM-RFE, random forest) selected core genes. A four-gene risk score model was constructed and validated in an independent cohort, with additional immune infiltration and drug-gene network analyses. In vitro experiments validated that SLC2A1 promotes PANC-1 cell proliferation, invasion, and NETs formation in neutrophil co-cultures. Four NETs-related genes (LAMC2, LAMB3, SLC2A1, ITGA2) were key prognostic markers for PC survival. The risk model showed strong predictive performance (AUC ~ 0.89 in training, > 0.90 in validation). High-risk tumors had more immunosuppressive cells and fewer effector T cells. Unsupervised clustering defined two PC subtypes with distinct metabolic and immune profiles. In vitro, elevated SLC2A1 in PANC-1 cells promoted proliferation, invasion, and NETs formation in neutrophil co-cultures. This multi-cohort analysis identifies a novel NETs-related four-gene signature and establishes a prognostic risk model for PC, highlighting the critical role of NETs biology in PC progression and provide a potential prognostic tool to facilitate patient stratification and guide precision oncology applications, with a foundation for future validation.
journal: Journal of environmental pathology, toxicology and oncology : official organ of the International Society for Environmental Toxicology and Cancer

title: Association of VISTA and BTLA polymorphisms with the risk of non-HBV and non-HCV related hepatocellular carcinoma in Western Guangxi, China: a pilot case-control study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Immune checkpoint including VISTA (V-domain Ig suppressor of T cell activation) and BTLA (B and T lymphocyte attenuator) critically regulate tumor immune evasion, and their genetic polymorphisms correlate multiple malignancies. With HBV vaccination and antiviral therapy advancing, non-B non-C hepatocellular carcinoma (NBNC-HCC) prevalence rises, while reliable early diagnosis biomarkers for NBNC-HCC remain lacking.
AIM: Thus, the present study investigates the associations between VISTA and BTLA polymorphisms and the risk of NBNC-HCC in western Guangxi, China, so as to facilitate targeted high-risk population screening for NBNC-HCC.
METHODS: A total of 125 NBNC-HCC patients and 150 healthy individuals were enrolled. Genotyping of VISTA (rs748113, rs10762477, rs3747862) and BTLA (rs3112270, rs1982809, rs1844089) was performed using multiplex PCR combined with targeted sequencing.
RESULTS: The AG vs AA, AG-GG vs AA, and allele G vs A of VISTA rs3747862, as well as the AA vs GG, GA-AA vs GG, AA vs GA-GG, and allele A vs G of BTLA rs1844089, were all associated with a significantly increased risk of NBNC-HCC (p < 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Given the relatively limited sample size and low statistical power, the observed associations between VISTA and BTLA polymorphisms and the risk of NBNC-HCC should be considered hypothesis-generating and require further systematic validation.

title: Exosome-Coated Dendrimer Nanogels as a Therapeutic Vaccine for CT Imaging-Guided Chemoimmunotherapy of Pancreatic Cancer.
abstract: Development of new medicines that can treat pancreatic cancer with a sustained immune memory effect remains to be a challenging task. Herein, we report a tumor microenvironment-responsive dendrimer nanogel (DNG)-based therapeutic vaccine co-loaded with toyocamycin (Toy) and gold nanoparticles (Au NPs) and the surface camouflaged with Cytosine-phosphate-Guanine (CpG)-functionalized exosomes derived from pancreatic cancer cells (termed as Au@DNG@C-Exo) for computed tomography (CT) imaging and chemoimmunotherapy of pancreatic cancer. The created Au@DNG@C-Exo through a reverse-phase microemulsion method displays a size of 105.6 nm with a narrow distribution, desired colloidal stability, and stimuli-responsive Toy release profile. We show that Au@DNG@C-Exo enables Exo-mediated homologous targeting chemotherapy of cancer cells to induce efficient immunogenic cell death (ICD), which synergizes with the CpG adjuvant/Exo antigen presentation to maturate dendritic cells (DCs), thereby initiating a potent antigen-specific anticancer immune response. Concurrently, the incorporated Au NPs repolarize tumor-associated macrophages from the M2 to the antitumor M1 phenotype and serve as contrast agents for CT imaging of tumors in vivo. The Au@DNG@C-Exo-mediated chemoimmunotherapy maximally suppresses the growth of Panc-02 tumors in a mouse model and elicits a robust systemic anti-tumor immune response. Meanwhile, Au@DNG@C-Exo also effectively prevents tumor occurrence after immunization. The developed DNG-based therapeutic nanovaccine that is able to modulate triple cell types, including cancer cells, DCs, and macrophages, presents a promising theranostic strategy to tackle pancreatic cancer.

title: Mechanisms of Resistance and Immune-Related Adverse Events Associated with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but their clinical benefits are constrained by primary and acquired resistance and immune-related adverse events (irAEs). Understanding the biological processes underlying these outcomes is essential for improving treatment efficacy and safety. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on ICI resistance and irAEs in HCC across tumor-intrinsic, microenvironmental, and systemic dimensions. Primary resistance involves impaired tumor antigen presentation, dysregulated oncogenic signaling, limited immune-cell infiltration, metabolic immunosuppression, and systemic immune dysfunction, with additional influences from the gut microbiota and underlying liver disease. Acquired resistance may involve immunoediting and clonal escape, compensatory inhibitory checkpoint signaling, and treatment-associated immunosuppressive remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. Mechanisms potentially contributing to irAEs include loss of peripheral immune tolerance, T-cell-mediated tissue injury, dysregulated inflammatory cytokine production, antigenic cross-reactivity, and autoantibody-associated immune dysregulation. The strength of evidence varies substantially across these mechanisms: several are supported by experimental HCC models and clinical observations, whereas others remain largely extrapolated from non-HCC settings or lack causal validation. Future priorities include integrating baseline and longitudinal tumor and host immune profiling to develop predictive biomarkers, detect emerging resistance, and identify patients at increased risk of severe toxicity. Prospective HCC-specific studies are needed to determine whether mechanism-guided interventions can improve outcomes. A more precise understanding of antitumor immunity and tissue tolerance may inform individualized strategies that sustain tumor control while preserving liver function and minimizing immune-related toxicity.

title: Mapping the Intellectual Architecture of Inflammation-Centered Macrophage Research in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Dual-Database Bibliometric and Scientometric Analysis, 2005-2025.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic liver inflammation provides a major biological context for hepatocarcinogenesis, and macrophages link innate immune sensing, fibrogenesis, immune suppression and therapeutic resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), Kupffer cells and inflammation-associated myeloid populations have been extensively investigated in HCC; however, the intellectual structure and thematic connectivity of this inflammation-centered research field remain incompletely defined.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to map the intellectual architecture, evolutionary trajectory and inter-module connectivity of inflammation-centered macrophage research in HCC using bibliometric and scientometric methods.
METHODS: A total of 9218 English-language articles and reviews on macrophage-related HCC from 2005 to 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus after systematic deduplication. CiteSpace, VOSviewer and bibliometrix were used to perform co-citation clustering, reference historiographic mapping, keyword co-occurrence analysis, publication-volume-adjusted keyword correlation analysis, citation burst detection, journal dual-map overlay and multi-level collaboration profiling.
RESULTS: Annual publication output increased from 84 articles in 2005 to 1129 in 2025. Co-citation analysis resolved 13 well-defined clusters (modularity Q = 0.744; mean silhouette S = 0.884), and historiographic mapping identified four sequential stages: foundational inflammation and hepatocarcinogenesis, mechanistic expansion of TAM function, immune-regulatory convergence and spatial immunology. Keyword dynamics showed a transition from viral hepatitis, innate immunity, Kupffer cells and fibroinflammatory terminology toward TAM-mediated immune suppression, immunotherapy, single-cell analysis, SPP1-positive macrophage-associated spatial immune barriers and computational precision oncology. After annual publication-volume adjustment, the foundational viral-innate module and the contemporary computational-precision oncology module showed a negative inter-module Pearson correlation (mean r = -0.383), lower than expected under label-permutation and temporal-succession null models (both p < 0.001). Three low-connectivity literature interfaces emerged: etiology-immunotherapy, TAM-organized spatial immune exclusion and TAM-MDSC shared myeloid biology.
CONCLUSION: Macrophage-related HCC research has evolved from inflammation-centered hepatocarcinogenesis toward spatially resolved and computationally assisted immunology. The low-connectivity interfaces identified in this study should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating bibliometric signals rather than as evidence of biological or clinical disconnection or as stand-alone research priorities derived from network structure alone. Their potential translational relevance should be considered alongside published mechanistic and clinical evidence and requires future mechanistic, spatial and prospective clinical validation.

Xiaoyao San enhances the sensitivity of hepatocellular carcinoma to 5-fluorouracilautophagy modulation.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the therapeutic potential of combining Xiaoyao San (XYS, ) aqueous extract with 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) in chemoresistant hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells.
METHODS: The effects of XYS on 5-FU-induced apoptosis and autophagy in Bel-7402/5-FU cell line were assessed using cell counting kit-8 (CCK8) assays, Western blotting, immunofluorescence, and transmission electron microscopy. A nude mouse xenograft model of human HCC was established to examine the in vivoeffects of XYS on tumor growth, as well as molecular alterations associated with apoptosis and autophagy. In addition, autophagy-related gene-5 (ATG5)-overexpressing and ATG5-silenced cell models were generated to further investigate the role of XYS in modulating 5-FU-induced apoptosis.
RESULTS: XYS enhanced the anti-proliferative effects of 5-FU and promoted apoptosis in chemoresistant HCC cells. These synergistic effects were further confirmed in vivo, where XYS potentiated the tumor-suppressive activity of 5-FU. Mechanistically, 5-FU treatment elevated basal autophagy, contributing to drug resistance, whereas XYS suppressed autophagy activation, thereby restoring sensitivity to 5-FU.
CONCLUSION: In HCC, 5-FU resistance appears to be mediated, at least in part, by drug-induced autophagy. XYS effectively inhibited autophagy and enhanced the chemosensitivity of HCC cells to 5-FU. These findings suggest that XYS may serve as a promising adjunctive therapy to improve the efficacy of 5-FU in treating HCC.

title: NIR-II emissive nanomedicine of dimer-structured conjugated oligomer induces immunogenic cell death for photoimmunotherapy of pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer is a highly immunosuppressive "cold" tumor that typically fails to achieve satisfactory immunotherapy outcomes. Photoimmunotherapy represents a preeminent cancer treatment strategy that combines the advantages of noninvasive phototherapy and drug-free immunotherapy. However, recently reported phototherapeutic materials predominantly respond to visible light via the oxygen-dependent pathway, severely weakening their efficacy in hypoxic and deep-seated tumors. Herein, a dimerization strategy for a near-infrared II (NIR-II)-emissive luminophore is developed for efficient image-guided photoimmunotherapy of "cold" pancreatic tumors. Owing to their dimeric design, the nanoparticles (NPs) of the dimeric luminophore (d-NBT) exhibited improved absorption and NIR-II fluorescence emission, along with efficient type-I reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and sufficient photothermal conversion performance under 808 nm light irradiation. With NIR-II imaging, d-NBT NPs have been demonstrated to provide high-resolution whole-body angiography beyond 1500 nm and efficient tumor accumulation. The complete ablation of pancreatic tumors in primary and KPC tumor models were achieved via the photoimmunotherapy effect of d-NBT NPs. This study provides a dimerization strategy for high-performance NIR-II emissive luminophores for imaging-guided photoimmunotherapy of "cold" pancreatic cancer.

title: Intravital Multiphoton Microscopy of Schwann Cells in Mouse Models of Pancreatic Disease.
abstract: Over the past decade, the important role of nerves in the growth and progression of pancreatic cancer has been increasingly recognized. The most abundant cell type present in the nerves, Schwann cells (SCs), can be reprogrammed by cancer cells and fibrotic extracellular matrix (ECM), facilitating perineural invasion of cancer cells in the pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Activated SCs form tracks, which are then populated and used by cancer cells for invasion. Intravital microscopy of the pancreas under the pathological conditions holds the potential to visualize and decipher real-time interactions of SCs with the cancer cells, ECM, and host cells in the tumor microenvironment and to delineate SC activation dynamics and the responses to targeted therapies. Here, we describe a protocol for high-resolution intravital microscopy of Schwann cells, ECM, and cancer cells using mouse models of PDAC or pancreatitis.

title: Combining locoregional treatments and immunotherapies in patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: The systemic treatment landscape of unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma has been transformed by immune-checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based regimens. These advances have led to efforts to combine ICIs with locoregional therapies (LRTs), particularly transarterial chemoembolization, transarterial radioembolization and external beam radiotherapy, in an attempt to improve tumour control and extend the benefits of ICIs to patients with intermediate-stage disease. The rationale for this combination approach is provided by the ability of LRTs to induce immunogenic cell death and tumour antigen release and to reprogramme the immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment. Five phase III trials have thus far shown improvements in progression-free survival and objective response rates with regimens combining ICIs with transarterial chemoembolization. Early-phase and real-world data also support the combination of ICIs with transarterial radioembolization or external beam radiotherapy, particularly in selected patients with focal disease unsuitable for embolization or portal vein tumour thrombosis. However, various challenges remain, including patient selection and therapy sequencing, response assessment, and the growing difficulties in demonstrating survival advantages in the context of widespread post-progression crossover and effective subsequent therapies. In this Review, we describe the biological rationale, summarize the clinical evidence and discuss future directions for trial design, imaging and biomarker-driven patient selection in the integration of LRTs with immune-based regimens for patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma.

title: Targeting PSMD14 increases chemotherapeutic sensitivity to gemcitabine by inhibiting the WNT/β-catenin pathway and glycolysis in pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Chemotherapy resistance is one of the important reasons for the low 5-year survival rate of patients with pancreatic cancer. Elucidating the mechanism of chemotherapy resistance is an important breakthrough direction for improving the prognosis. Here, PSMD14, a deubiquitinating enzyme frequently overexpressed in human pancreatic cancer, was demonstrated to mediate chemoresistance principally by activating the WNT/β-catenin pathway. Mechanistically, PSMD14 activated the WNT/β-catenin pathway by removing the K63-linked ubiquitination of DVL1 and promoting its translocation from the cytoplasm to the membrane, consequently facilitating the aerobic glycolysis and contributing to the chemoresistance of pancreatic cancer cells. Furthermore, activation of the WNT/β-catenin pathway promoted the transcription of PSMD14, and the PSMD14 inhibitor capzimin improved the sensitivity of pancreatic cancer cells to gemcitabine in cells, organoids, and mouse models. In conclusion, PSMD14 plays a critical role in regulating the activity of WNT/β-catenin and the sensitivity of pancreatic cancer to gemcitabine, suggesting that PSMD14 appears to be a promising therapeutic target for pancreatic cancer.

title: Autophagy and intratumoral bacteria abundance influence the prognosis of patients with pancreatic carcinoma.
abstract: The biological and clinical significance of the intratumoral microbiota in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains poorly defined. Using oncogenic Kras-driven mouse models of pancreatic tumorigenesis and human pancreatic tissue from patients with non-metastatic PDAC treated with neoadjuvant (n = 62) or adjuvant therapy (n = 101), along with samples from intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMN, n = 24), chronic pancreatitis (CP, n = 33), and healthy donors (n = 9), we determined tissue lipopolysaccharide (LPS), 16S rRNA sequencing, high-resolution quantitative multiplex immunofluorescence of autophagy markers (LAMP2, LC3B) and LPS, 16S rRNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) staining, and TLR4 signaling. In KrasCre mice, we identified significant bacterial accumulation in the pancreas, indicated by elevated LPS, increased FISH signals, enhanced TLR4 signaling, and activation of autophagy. Administration of exogenous LPS further amplified autophagy and TLR4 signaling, supporting a mechanistic link between microbial sensing and autophagy. In human tissue, both adjuvant and neoadjuvant PDAC samples showed significantly increased bacterial alpha- and beta diversity compared with controls, while CP showed a similar enrichment pattern that IPMN lacks; the underlying microbial diversity differs fundamentally across these conditions. Increased LPS levels, along with elevated autophagy markers and abundant FISH-positive bacteria, support the presence of intratumoral bacteria. Across four independent transcriptomic datasets, PDAC samples showed elevated expression of bacteria-associated pathways (including TLR4) and autophagy-related genes. Clinically, higher autophagy-associated LAMP2-LC3B colocalization and increased densities of FISH-positive cells were independently associated with prolonged survival in both adjuvant and neoadjuvant or combined PDAC patients. Collectively, these findings link intratumoral microbial enrichment to increased autophagy-associated signaling and improved patient outcomes, suggesting that microbial signals within the tumor microenvironment were associated with favorable survival.

title: Co-delivery of Sorafenib and Anti-miR-21 via a CD44-guided Nanocarrier for Dual-pathway Inhibition in HCC Cells.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/AIM: The clinical efficacy of sorafenib against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is severely limited by limited efficacy and off-target toxicity. Overexpression of oncogenic miR-21 has been identified as a key driver of these limitations, as it downregulates the tumor suppressors PTEN and PDCD4, thereby aberrantly activating both the PI3K/Akt and STAT3 signaling pathways. To address the limitations of conventional sorafenib therapy, we aimed to construct a smart nanocarrier capable of simultaneously delivering sorafenib (SF) and anti-miR-21 specifically to HCC cells.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We designed a core-shell nanoparticle consisting of a PAMAM dendrimer/anti-miR-21 polyplex core and a hyaluronic acid-sorafenib conjugate shell. This architecture enables CD44-mediated active targeting and pH-responsive drug release in the acidic tumor microenvironment. The antitumor activity of the co-delivery system was evaluated in vitro using HepG2 cells, with assessments of cell proliferation, migration, apoptosis, and the underlying signaling pathways.
RESULTS: The prepared nanoparticle exhibited potent anti-proliferative, anti-migratory, and pro-apoptotic effects in HepG2 cells. Mechanistic studies revealed that these benefits were associated with the reduced phosphorylation of key proteins in both the PI3K/Akt/mTOR and STAT3 cascades, effectively counteracting the therapy limitations that are normally fueled by miR-21 overexpression.
CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrate that CD44-guided co-delivery of sorafenib and anti-miR-21 provides a promising nanotherapeutic strategy to counteract therapy limitations through coordinated blockade of two major oncogenic pathways in HCC cells.

title: Glycolysis-related hub genes associated with shared resistance signatures to TACE and PD-1 therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) and immune checkpoint inhibitors are the mainstay treatments for intermediate and advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet resistance to both remains a major clinical challenge. Whether these two resistance modalities share common molecular mediators remains largely unknown.
METHODS: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) associated with TACE resistance (GSE104580) and anti-PD-1 resistance (GSE202069) were intersected. Common DEGs underwent enrichment analysis, protein-protein interaction network construction, and hub gene identification (cytoHubba MCC). Expression, prognostic value, and immune infiltration correlations were validated using GEPIA2, UALCAN, and TIMER3.
RESULTS: We identified 117 common DEGs, with glycolysis/gluconeogenesis and HIF-1 signaling significantly enriched. Seven hub genes were pinpointed: PKM, PCK1, ALDOB, SLC2A1, ENO2, PFKFB1, and HK2. High expression of glycolytic genes (PKM, SLC2A1, ENO2, HK2) and low expression of gluconeogenic genes (PCK1, ALDOB) predicted poor overall survival. Immune infiltration analysis revealed a pattern consistent with a "hot but suppressed" phenotype: glycolytic hubs correlated with enriched MDSCs, regulatory T cells, and macrophages despite concurrent CD8+ T-cell infiltration, whereas gluconeogenic hubs showed the opposite pattern.
CONCLUSIONS: Glycolysis-related hub genes, particularly PKM, are associated with shared resistance signatures to TACE and immunotherapy resistance in HCC and may serve as exploratory biomarkers for treatment response. Given the small immunotherapy-response cohort and the correlative nature of the analyses, these findings require independent validation and functional testing before clinical translation.
journal: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry

title: Fucoidan-functionalized liposomal nanocarriers for targeted miR-217-5p delivery and combined antitumor treatment in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
abstract: The clinical translation of microRNA (miRNA) therapy is hindered by poor tumor specificity and inefficient delivery. In this study, we constructed a targeted nanoplatform using marine sulfated polysaccharide fucoidan (FU) to encapsulate miR-217-5p in FU-modified cationic liposomes (FU-LIP-miR) for the treatment of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), alone or in combination with gemcitabine (GEM). In this system, FU serves primarily as a targeting ligand. FU was incorporated as a functional surface ligand. Previous studies have demonstrated a high-affinity interaction between FU and P-selectin, suggesting that this interaction may contribute to the enhanced tumor-associated accumulation of FU-functionalized nanocarriers. Furthermore, FU is susceptible to degradation by H2O2 within the tumor microenvironment, consequently enabling controlled drug release. Initial findings confirmed that that miR-217-5p was significantly downregulated in PDAC tissues. FU-LIP-miR promoted the tumor accumulation and delivery of miR-217-5p and restored its expression, which was accompanied by reduced PDAC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Notably, FU can also be employed as an active targeting ligand. FU-LIP-miR combined with GEM produced an enhanced antitumor effect and increased apoptosis in PDAC cells. In a subcutaneous xenograft model using Panc02 cells in C57BL/6 mice, the combination of FU-LIP-miR and GEM produced enhanced antitumor efficacy compared with the corresponding control treatments. This study underscores the pivotal role of FU as a versatile polysaccharide in the design of targeted delivery platforms, thereby providing a novel and promising noncoding RNA-based therapeutic approach for PDAC using polysaccharide materials.

title: KRASG12D-targeted therapy sensitivity depends on interferon signaling activation in pancreatic cancer.
abstract: KRASG12D is a predominant driver in pancreatic cancer, yet the basis of intrinsic resistance to KRASG12D-targeted therapy remains poorly defined. Integrated genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics profiling across 242 patient-derived organoids (PDOs) and matched tumor tissues reveals a KRASG12D-mutant subset intrinsically resistant to KRASG12D-targeted therapeutics, characterized by marked downregulation of innate immune signaling pathways. Functional validation demonstrates that suppressing interferon signaling in sensitive models induces resistance, whereas activation of interferon signaling, particularly interferon beta (IFN-β), increases sensitivity in resistant models. Combining IFN-β with KRAS inhibitors (MRTX1133, HRS-4642, and RMC-6236) exhibits synergistic antitumor effects in intrinsically resistant pancreatic cancer. Mechanistically, sustained MYC activity is associated with attenuated sensitivity to KRAS inhibition and correlates with repressed interferon signaling, suggesting a potential role in promoting intrinsic resistance. These findings identify interferon signaling as a candidate determinant of KRAS-targeted therapy response and support interferon-based combinations as a potential strategy for intrinsically resistant pancreatic cancer.

title: Intrinsic resistance to KRAS inhibition: Interfering with interferon.
abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Zhang et al. perform multi-omics profiling on a large collection of patient-derived pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma organoids to elucidate the mechanisms underlying intrinsic resistance to KRAS inhibition. This work identifies suppression of innate immune signaling through sustained MYC activity as the principal driver of intrinsic resistance.

title: Tumor-derived amyloid-β drives TREM2+ macrophages immunosuppression in cholangiocarcinoma.
abstract: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is an aggressive malignancy with limited therapeutic options. In this study, we explored the role of TREM2+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) in modulating the immune microenvironment and their impact on anti-PD-1 therapy. Using single-cell RNA sequencing data and immunohistochemical analysis, we identified a significant upregulation of TREM2 in TAMs in human CCA, correlating with decreased CD8+ T cell infiltration and poor prognosis. TREM2 deficiency in a mouse model of CCA led to a reprogramming of TAMs to a pro-inflammatory phenotype, with a marked increase in CD86+ macrophages and a significant reduction in CD206+ macrophages. This phenotypic shift enhanced the recruitment and activity of CD8+ T cells, driving a potent pro-inflammatory immune response. Additionally, we uncovered that Aβ produced by CCA cells contributes to TAM polarization through TREM2/PI3K/AKT1 signaling pathway. Blocking Aβ signaling further augmented TAM reprogramming and CD8+ T cell infiltration. The combination of TREM2 deletion and Aβ inhibition significantly enhanced the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy, resulting in reduced tumor growth, increased survival, and improved overall therapeutic outcomes in both subcutaneous and hydrodynamic tail vein CCA models. These findings suggest that targeting TREM2 and Aβ in conjunction with anti-PD-1 immunotherapy holds promise as a novel therapeutic strategy for CCA.
